title: Palate
description: Conditions affecting the hard and soft palate — the roof of the mouth — including candidal infections under dentures, bony outgrowths, smoking-related keratosis, dental abscesses pointing palatally, and salivary gland swellings.

problems.description: Uniform redness of the palatal mucosa under an upper denture. Patient often unaware because there is no pain.
problems.etiology:
Candida albicans is responsible in 90% of cases, with most of the remaining 9% caused by other Candida species [1]. The fungus exploits conditions under the denture: poor denture hygiene, continuous wear including overnight, and a high-carbohydrate diet that gives Candida substrate to multiply [2]. The denture itself acts as a reservoir — once the fitting surface is colonised, cleaning the mucosa alone will not clear the infection [2].

Systemic factors can lower the threshold for infection: iron and vitamin deficiency, steroid use, drugs that cause xerostomia, and endocrine abnormalities [2]. Trauma is sometimes cited as a cause but the evidence is weak — the condition occurs under well-fitting orthodontic appliances too, and is found under an upper denture even when no lower denture is worn [2].
problems.presentation:
The patient usually presents without a complaint about the palate itself. The condition is asymptomatic and not normally noticed by patients [3]. It comes to light on examination when the denture is removed: the palatal mucosa under the fitting surface looks uniformly red, with petechial or whitish areas in some cases [1].

The surrounding uncovered palate looks normal by contrast. Look at the commissures too — angular cheilitis commonly coexists [1].
problems.results:
- **Visual appearance** is often enough for a working diagnosis: uniform erythema confined precisely to the denture-bearing area, stopping at the denture border.
- **Swab of the fitting surface** confirms Candida species if needed; speciation guides antifungal choice in resistant cases.
- **Haematinics and blood glucose** if the infection involves other sites beyond the denture footprint, or if treatment fails despite good denture hygiene [4]. Diabetes and iron deficiency both predispose.
- **Denture assessment**: check hygiene, assess whether the patient wears it overnight, note fit and age of the prosthesis.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key tell is the strict anatomical boundary — the redness matches the denture footprint exactly. That pattern does not occur with erythematous candidosis from antibiotics or inhaled steroids, which is more diffuse [5].

Unlike papillary hyperplasia (which can co-exist), the surface is flat and atrophic rather than nodular. Unlike a traumatic ulcer, there is no break in the mucosa and no pain.
problems.treatment:
Four elements run together [2]:

- **Leave dentures out at night.** Night-time wear is a major driver; removing the denture breaks the cycle.
- **Denture hygiene**: brush the fitting surface and soak in a hypochlorite cleanser daily. The denture harbours the Candida and must be treated alongside the mucosa [2].
- **Miconazole gel** applied to the fitting surface before insertion covers Candida and the bacterial co-infectors. Miconazole oral gel 24mg/mL: apply a pea-sized amount after food qds [6]. Check for drug interactions — miconazole raises INR in patients on warfarin and interacts with antidiabetics, antiepileptics, and antihistamines [7].
- **Systemic fluconazole** if topical measures fail [2].

If papillary hyperplasia has developed under the denture, surgical reduction may be needed [2]. If denture hygiene is good and the condition persists, refer to the GP to exclude systemic predisposition [4].

Reduce sugar intake as an adjunct [2].
problems.prognosis: With improved denture hygiene and overnight removal, the mucosa recovers. Without fixing the denture habits, topical antifungals give only temporary relief because the colonised fitting surface reinfects the mucosa [4]. Recurrent or treatment-resistant cases almost always have either ongoing denture wear at night or an unaddressed systemic predisposing factor.

citations.quote: Also known as denture sore mouth, a misnomer because the condition is usually symptomless. Classically, seen as redness of the palate under a F/− denture, with petechial and whitish areas. 90% of cases due to Candida albicans, 9% to other Candida spp., and <1% to other organisms, e.g. Klebsiella spp.

Night-time wear of dentures. Trauma is often cited as a contributing factor to denture stomatitis, but: It occurs more commonly under F/− than −/F. It can affect patients wearing F/− only. It is also found under well-fitting orthodontic appliances. Systemic factors can predispose to Candida infection, e.g. iron and vitamin deficiency, steroids, drugs which cause xerostomia, and endocrine abnormalities. A high sugar intake provides substrate for Candida to multiply. Patients should be encouraged to remove their dentures at night. They should cleanse denture thoroughly, e.g. brushing fitting surface and soaking in hypochlorite cleanser. New dentures may be required if these measures fail despite good compliance. The denture can act as a reservoir for Candida. Reduce sugar intake. Miconazole gel can be added to the fitting surface of the denture before insertion. Coexisting papillary hyperplasia of palate may need surgical reduction. Systemic fluconazole may be used in some cases.
Redness of the denture-bearing area almost certainly indicates denture stomatitis (chronic atrophic candidosis). However, this condition is asymptomatic and not normally noticed by patients.

To solve the denture problem, the denture must be remade with an appropriate freeway space, but the denture stomatitis must first be treated to improve support for the new prosthesis. Treatment will involve improving denture hygiene, ceasing night wear, if appropriate. The possibility of an underlying condition predisposing to candidosis should be considered, especially if the infection involves other parts of the mouth or lips or if treatment fails despite good denture hygiene. In this case, referral to the patient's general practitioner would be indicated for further investigations.

This is an opportunistic infection following the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, sometimes inhaled steroids, and in patients with HIV as well as those with xerostomia. It is painful and exacerbated by hot or spicy foods. The oral mucosa has a red, shiny, atrophic appearance and there may be coexisting areas of thrush.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 6040 (erythematous candidosis — contrast condition)

citations.quote: Miconazole oral gel 24mg/mL is of use in chronic mucocutaneous and chronic hyperplastic candidosis. Dose: 2.5mL qds 20mg/g gel. Apply a pea-sized amount after food qds. Can be applied to dentures also.

There are recognized potentially serious interactions between miconazole, fluconazole, and related drugs and antibacterials, anticoagulants, antidiabetics, antiepileptics, antihistamines, anxiolytics, cisapride, ciclosporin, and theophylline. Check what your patient is currently taking.

problems.description: Hard, smooth, immovable bony swelling running along the midline of the hard palate. Noticed incidentally. No symptoms.
problems.etiology: A developmental bony exostosis arising from the midline of the hard palate [1]. The precise cause is not fully understood — it is a normal variant, not a pathological process. It causes no harm and is not part of any syndrome [1].
problems.presentation:
Most patients are unaware of it or have noticed a hard lump they assumed was normal. No pain, no ulceration. The swelling sits in the centre of the hard palate, typically oval or lobulated, covered with normal-looking mucosa that may be thin over the crest.

Occasionally the patient presents because a new denture has identified it — the prominence blocks the fitting surface.
problems.results:
- **Palpation**: hard as bone, non-tender, immovable, smooth surface.
- **Radiograph** not usually needed, but when taken it shows a radiopaque mass continuous with the palatal bone.
- No vitality involvement, no lymphadenopathy.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Torus palatinus sits strictly in the midline of the hard palate — that position is distinctive [1]. A palatal abscess from a dental infection is off-midline, is fluctuant, and the causative tooth will be non-vital. A salivary gland tumour is typically lateral (posterior palate) and soft to fluctuant, not bone-hard. Torus is bone-hard and midline; those two features together essentially clinch the diagnosis without further investigation.
problems.treatment: Reassurance that this developmental anomaly causes no harm [1]. No treatment is needed in most cases. Rarely, excision is indicated when the torus prevents construction of a satisfactory upper denture [1] — in that case refer to oral surgery.
problems.prognosis: The torus is benign and static. Once identified and explained to the patient, no further management is needed. If excision is carried out for prosthetic reasons, the result is good.

citations.quote: These are bony exostoses found in both jaws. Torus palatinus is found in the centre of the hard palate; torus mandibularis on the lingual premolar/molar region of the mandible. Rx: reassurance that these developmental anomalies cause no harm (they are not part of the Gardener syndrome). Rarely, excision for denture construction is indicated.

problems.description: White or grey palatal mucosa covered in raised red papules, each with a dark central dot. Found in a pipe or heavy cigarette smoker.
problems.etiology: Caused by a combination of the low-grade thermal burn and chemical irritants in tobacco smoke [2]. Affects the hard palate specifically because palate-directed smoke is concentrated there in pipe and cigar smokers, and in very heavy cigarette smokers [1, 2]. The minor salivary glands respond to the chronic insult by dilating their duct openings, which accounts for the visible red papular dots [1].
problems.presentation:
Patient is typically a pipe or cigar smoker, or a very heavy cigarette smoker. The palate looks white-grey with multiple small red papules. Each papule has a dark central head, which is the dilated opening of a minor salivary gland duct [1]. Usually asymptomatic — found on routine examination.

Note: the similar-sounding smoker's keratosis is a separate entity and affects non-keratinized buccal, tongue, or palatal mucosa without the papular pattern [2].
problems.results:
- **Visual appearance** is often diagnostic: white/grey palatal base with red-centred papules concentrated on the hard palate [1].
- No specific tests required for the palatal lesion itself, but the presence of stomatitis nicotina should prompt assessment of higher-risk sites: floor of mouth, retro-molar region, and lateral tongue [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The papular pattern — numerous discrete red dots on a white-grey base — is distinctive and seen virtually nowhere else in the mouth [1]. The strict localisation to the hard palate, combined with a clear smoking history, separates it from erythematous candidosis (which is more diffuse and not papular) and from denture stomatitis (which is under the denture, not pattern-forming). The dark central dot (dilated gland opening) is the defining histological-clinical feature [1].

The important clinical point: stomatitis nicotina itself has little evidence of being premalignant at the palate, but it signals tobacco use and should prompt examination of genuinely high-risk sites — floor of mouth, lateral tongue, retro-molar [1].
problems.treatment: Smoking cessation is the treatment. The white/grey appearance of smoker's keratosis resolves on stopping smoking [2]. Advise cessation, examine high-risk mucosal sites at the same visit, and re-examine after a cessation attempt to ensure resolution.
problems.prognosis: The lesion resolves on stopping smoking [2]. Continued smoking maintains the condition and keeps the patient at risk of pathology at higher-risk sites. The palatal lesion itself is not strongly associated with malignant change, but it is a marker of tobacco exposure to the rest of the oral mucosa [1].

citations.quote: Affects palate; numerous red papules on a white/grey base. The papules have a dark 'head' which is the opening of a distended minor salivary gland. May indicate a risk of dysplasia or neoplasm at high-risk sites such as floor of mouth, retro-molar region, or lateral tongue.

Characteristically a white patch affecting buccal mucosa, tongue, or palate. Due to a combination of low-grade burn and the chemical irritants of smoke, and seen particularly in pipe smokers. There is little evidence that these patches are premalignant and they resolve on stopping smoking.

problems.description: Palatal swelling or sinus discharging pus. The tooth pointing to it is tender and non-vital. Patient may report a salty taste.
problems.conditionName: Palatal dental abscess (apical infection draining palatally)
problems.etiology: Apical infection from a non-vital tooth tracks through bone and periosteum until it finds the path of least resistance. Palatal roots of upper molars and the roots of upper lateral incisors are anatomically close to the palatal cortex, so abscess from these teeth discharges palatally rather than buccally [1]. The causative tooth has necrotic pulp — from caries, trauma, or failed endodontic treatment.
problems.presentation:
What the patient typically describes:

- A tender swelling on the roof of the mouth, often with a salty or unpleasant taste as the pus discharges.
- The tooth itself may ache or be sore to bite on; sometimes the pain has recently eased (when pus found an exit route).

What you see:

- A fluctuant or pointing swelling on the palate, off-midline, aligned with the causative root.
- A sinus opening discharging pus in some cases.
- The responsible tooth is typically discoloured, crowned, has a large restoration, or has a history of trauma [1].
problems.results:
- **Vitality testing**: causative tooth will be non-vital.
- **Percussion**: tooth is tender to percussion (TTP); this may be diminished once pus has tracked and decompressed [1].
- **Periapical radiograph**: shows periapical radiolucency at the palatal root of the offending tooth. For upper molars, this may mean the palatal root specifically.
- **Palpation**: swelling is fluctuant when pus is present; firm and tender in early cellulitic stage.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The diagnostic triangle is: non-vital tooth + palatal swelling in the same quadrant + radiographic periapical change at the root pointing palatally.

Contrast with:

- **Periodontal abscess**: probing depth >3mm alongside the tooth, tooth usually vital, no periapical radiographic change.
- **Torus palatinus**: midline, bone-hard, the adjacent teeth are vital.
- **Salivary gland swelling**: slow-growing, painless, no vitality change in the teeth [2].
problems.treatment:
Drain the pus, then address the tooth [1]. Drainage options:

- **Via the root canal** if endodontic treatment is planned.
- **Incision of the fluctuant abscess** under LA: infiltrate LA between the abscess cavity and overlying mucosa, incise, explore with blunt closed forceps, and keep the incision patent — either by excising an ellipse of tissue or suturing in a small rubber drain. The rubber drain is particularly important in the palate because the tight palatal mucosa closes rapidly [1].
- **Extraction** if the tooth is unrestorable.

Antibiotic cover for the procedure: amoxicillin 500mg tds PO for 5–7 days, or metronidazole 400mg tds PO for 5–7 days, or both. For severe infections with systemic involvement, in-patient management with extraoral drainage may be needed [1].
problems.prognosis: With drainage and treatment of the causative tooth (RCT or extraction), the abscess resolves and the palatal swelling subsides. Without treatment, the infection continues, the sinus becomes chronic, and there is ongoing bone destruction around the root apex.

citations.quote: Teeth with an apical abscess are TTP and non-vital. They may be discoloured or crowned and have a history of trauma or RCT. Pain and TTP are often diminished when the intrabony pus tracks through the soft tissues and discharges, usually in the buccal sulcus (exceptions are 2, and palatal roots of maxillary molars which discharge palatally, and 12— which often discharge on the chin). Drainage of pus either via the root canal, by incision of any fluctuant abscess, or by extraction under LA or GA. Palatal or buccal abscesses can be drained quite simply under LA by infiltrating a small amount of LA between the abscess cavity and the overlying mucosa, then incising the abscess. Explore using blunt closed forceps and keep patent either by excising an ellipse of tissue or inserting and suturing a small rubber drain; this is particularly important in the palate. Cover the procedure with 'best guess' antibiotics such as amoxicillin 500mg tds PO for 5–7 days, or metronidazole 400mg tds PO for 5–7 days, or both. For severe infections, in-patient management with EO drainage may be needed.

Dental causes must be considered because they are very common. The site would be highly typical for an abscess arising from a nonvital lateral incisor or the palatal root of an upper first molar, but there are no symptoms or signs of acute infection. The slow and painless growth might suggest a cyst as a likely cause.
citations.source: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving · paragraph 6035 (palatal swelling differential)

problems.description: Slow-growing, painless, firm swelling on the lateral hard palate or posterior soft palate. No dental cause found and teeth are vital.
problems.conditionName: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland (palatal)
problems.etiology: Minor salivary glands are distributed throughout the oral mucosa but are particularly dense in the posterior hard palate and lips [1]. A palatal swelling arising from these glands is most likely neoplastic when slow-growing and persistent. About 50% of minor gland neoplasms are benign and 50% are malignant [2]. The most common single benign tumour is pleomorphic adenoma [2]. Pleomorphic adenoma is often incompletely encapsulated, which means satellite tumour cells can lie outside the capsule — simple enucleation leaves these cells behind [3].
problems.presentation:
Patient notices a lump but reports no pain initially [4]. The swelling has been present for months to years and has enlarged slowly [4]. Over time, as it enlarges, it may begin to cause discomfort [4].

What you see: a firm, smooth, non-tender swelling on the lateral palate, typically level with or behind the molars [2]. Mucosa overlying it looks normal. No ulceration.
problems.results:
- **Palpation**: firm, smooth, not fluctuant, non-tender. Not bone-hard (distinguishes it from torus palatinus).
- **Vitality tests**: all upper teeth in the quadrant should be vital — non-vitality would point to a dental cause [5].
- **Periapical / occlusal radiograph**: no bony expansion or radiolucency expected from a minor gland tumour unless large; needed to exclude dental cause [5].
- **Fine-needle aspiration (FNAC)**: in a specialist setting, FNAC is used to confirm the diagnosis pre-operatively. Sheets of uniform epithelial cells with spindle cells in myxoid matrix are characteristic of pleomorphic adenoma [6].
- **Incisional or excision biopsy**: definitive diagnosis requires histology [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The combination of a lateral palatal location (posterior to the premolars), long slow history, firm but not bone-hard consistency, and vital neighbouring teeth points strongly to a salivary gland origin [2].

Contrast with:

- **Torus palatinus**: midline, bone-hard, present since young adulthood, no growth over months.
- **Palatal abscess**: tender, vital test abnormal, history of pain, often acute onset.
- **Mucous retention cyst**: would fluctuate or burst over such a long period; less likely to be firm [7].

Malignant salivary gland neoplasm is a serious alternative: mucoepidermoid carcinoma and polymorphous adenocarcinoma are the most common, with adenoid cystic carcinoma rarer but carrying a poorer prognosis [2]. The absence of ulceration and younger age favour benign, but malignant tumours can have a benign presentation [2].
problems.treatment:
Refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery. The appropriate treatment is excision with a small margin of at least a few millimetres [3]. Simple enucleation results in recurrence because of the incomplete capsulation [3]. The defect is closed with a temporary acrylic plate or local surgical flaps [3]. Radiotherapy is not used for primary benign disease [3].

Before excision, CT or CBCT may be indicated to check whether the palate has been perforated — any oronasal or oroantral fistula must be repaired at the time of surgery [8].
problems.prognosis: Complete excision with a clear margin is curative [3]. If excised histologically clear, cure can be expected [9]. Carcinomatous change (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) can arise in long-standing untreated tumours — typically after 10 or more years — and carries a very poor prognosis [10]. Early referral and excision before the tumour is large or long-standing avoids this risk [10].

citations.quote: The salivary glands consist of the major glands, the paired sublingual, submandibular, and parotid glands, and the minor salivary glands present throughout the oral mucosa, but which are particularly dense in the posterior palate and lips.

The site of the swelling is compatible with a palatal salivary gland origin, although it is slightly more anterior than is typical. Salivary glands are more numerous in the posterior hard palate or soft palate, and a swelling level with or behind the molars would be more characteristic of a salivary gland origin. If the lesion is arising in a gland, then a neoplasm is the most likely cause of long-standing painless swelling. About 50% of minor gland neoplasms are benign, and 50% are malignant. The most common single benign tumour, by far, is pleomorphic adenoma, and this is a very likely cause in this case. Malignant salivary gland neoplasms are equally common in minor glands, as noted above. If the tumour is malignant, then mucoepidermoid carcinoma or polymorphous adenocarcinoma would be the most likely causes because they are the most prevalent. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is rarer, but clinically significant possibility because it requires more extensive surgery and carries a poorer prognosis. The lack of ulceration and the patient's young age point to a benign neoplasm over a malignant one, but a malignant tumour is a definite possibility because most salivary gland malignant neoplasms are of low grade and can have a benign presentation.

The appropriate treatment is excision with a small margin, at least a few millimetres. Pleomorphic adenoma is benign, but it is often incompletely encapsulated, and simple enucleation would result in recurrence. The defect could be closed with either a temporary acrylic plate or local surgical flaps, depending on the surgeon's preference. Radiotherapy is ineffective as a primary treatment and would not be indicated for a benign neoplasm.
The patient thinks that the lump has been present for at least a year, possibly 2 years. It has enlarged slowly and is now starting to cause discomfort.

Tests of vitality of all the teeth in the upper right quadrant are required to exclude the possibility that a nonvital tooth is present and is the cause of an abscess or cyst. Radiographs are required for these and other reasons.

Fig. 55.2a shows a sheet of uniform cells with moderate amounts of cytoplasm. Their cytoplasm, polygonal shape and cohesive growth indicate that these are epithelial cells and their uniform nuclei suggest they are benign. The second field, shown in Fig. 55.2b, shows smaller numbers of spindle cells without significant cytoplasm in a myxoid matrix. Taken together, these appearances are characteristic of pleomorphic adenoma.

A mucous retention cyst is the most likely nonneoplastic, salivary gland–related cause, and the bluish tinge to the lesion suggests a cyst. However, this lump is firm and appears to be of long duration. A mucous retention cyst would be expected to burst or fluctuate in size if present over a long period.

Although the pleomorphic adenoma is benign, it can resorb bone by pressure. Before excising the lesion, it is important to know whether the palate has been perforated because any postsurgical oronasal or oroantral fistula would have to be repaired.
If the lesion appears excised histologically, cure can be expected.

Yes, carcinoma may arise in a long-standing pleomorphic adenoma, and carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma carries a very poor prognosis. However, this process takes many years, usually 10 or more, and is therefore seen mostly in older patients.

problems.description: Cleft of the palate with intact overlying mucosa — the defect is hidden until abnormal speech or feeding difficulty is noticed.
problems.etiology: Cleft palate can be classified as involving the primary palate, secondary palate, or both, and may be complete or incomplete, unilateral or bilateral [1]. Submucous cleft is the hidden variant: the overlying mucosa remains intact, so the underlying bony or muscular defect is not visible on simple inspection [1]. The aetiology is multifactorial — genetic and environmental factors both contribute, and the condition can occur in isolation or as part of a syndrome [2].
problems.presentation: What you'll often hear first is a parental concern about speech. Because the mucosa is intact, the diagnosis is missed until poor speech is noticed [1]. Feeding difficulties in infancy may be the first pointer. The palate looks superficially normal, which is why it is easily overlooked at routine examination.
problems.results: Isolated cleft palate occurs in approximately 1:2000 births, with females more commonly affected than males [3]. Congenital anomalies coexist in up to 20% of cleft palate cases [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason submucous cleft is missed is exactly what makes it distinctive: the mucosa is intact [1]. Overt cleft palate is visible immediately at birth; submucous cleft is found only when speech therapy or careful examination uncovers it.
problems.treatment: Refer to a specialist cleft team — management involves a cleft surgeon, ENT surgeon, speech therapist, orthodontist, and clinical psychologist working together [5]. Palatal closure is typically performed between 9 and 12 months of age, with the goal of preserving speech development [6]. Deferring repair reduces growth disturbance but adversely affects speech development [6].
problems.prognosis: Speech and hearing outcomes depend on early recognition and timely repair. In repaired clefts, maxillary growth is reduced in all three planes compared to unrepaired clefts, which show near-normal growth — so the timing and technique of repair are the key variables [7]. The takeaway is that missing the diagnosis until late childhood means suboptimal speech outcomes.

citations.quote: Many exist, but the best approach is to describe cleft: 1° &/or 2° palate; complete or incomplete; unilateral or bilateral. Submucous cleft of the palate is often missed until poor speech noticed, as overlying mucosa is intact.
Multifactorial with both genetic and environmental factors (including maternal smoking, alcohol, and phenytoin intake) involved. Can occur in isolation or as part of a syndrome.
Isolated cleft palate occurs in 1:2000 births. F > M. Family history in 20%.
These occur in up to 20% of cases with CLP and are more likely in association with isolated clefts of palate than lip.

Team usually includes cleft surgeon, ear, nose, and throat (ENT) surgeon, health visitors, orthodontist, speech therapist, clinical psychologist, and central coordinator. Centralization of care and audit of outcome gives better results.

Usually between 9 and 12 months. Delaire or Von Langenbeck ± modifications are the most popular. Deferring repair until patient is older ↓ growth disturbance, but speech development is adversely affected.
Unrepaired clefts show normal growth. In repaired clefts maxillary growth is ↓ AP, transversely, and vertically. Mandibular growth also d.

problems.description: Palatal mucosa under an old or ill-fitting upper denture develops a nodular, cobblestone surface — sometimes associated with angular cheilitis.
problems.conditionName: Inflammatory papillary hyperplasia of the palate
problems.etiology: Inflammatory papillary hyperplasia is one of the problems that emerges from denture neglect. As a denture ages and the ridge resorbs, the appliance becomes progressively ill-fitting, and the resulting movement in function can drive a combination of mucosal changes: resorption, Candida colonisation, denture irritation hyperplasia, and papillary hyperplasia of the palate [1].
problems.presentation:
Usually found incidentally when examining the palate under a long-worn denture. The patient may have no complaint about the palate itself. What you see on removing the denture is an irregular, nodular surface — small papillary projections covering all or part of the palate under the denture footprint.

Denture hygiene is typically poor.
problems.results:
- **Visual inspection** under the denture is the key finding: raised papillary nodules on the palatal mucosa, confined to the denture-bearing area.
- **No special investigations** are needed for the diagnosis itself, but the condition signals a need for review of Candida status (swab the fitting surface) and investigation of systemic predisposition if the infection is widespread [3].
- **Denture assessment**: check occlusal surface wear, fit, and the patient's night-wear habits — all are likely to be abnormal.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit is how this differs from denture stomatitis proper: both occur under an ill-fitting denture and both have a Candida component, but papillary hyperplasia is nodular rather than uniformly erythematous and flat [2][4]. The cobblestone texture is the distinguishing surface feature. Unlike a simple candidal infection, the papillary overgrowth may not fully resolve with antifungals alone — surgical reduction may be needed [2].
problems.treatment: Start with the same measures as denture stomatitis: night-time denture removal, thorough fitting-surface hygiene, reduced sugar intake, and miconazole gel applied to the fitting surface [2]. If the papillary hyperplasia persists despite good compliance, surgical reduction may be required before new dentures can be constructed [2].
problems.prognosis: With good denture hygiene and antifungal treatment the mucosal inflammation improves, but established papillary overgrowth often requires surgical reduction before the palate returns to a suitable denture-bearing surface [2]. New dentures should only be made once the palate has settled.

citations.quote: As a result of resorption all dentures become progressively ill-fitting, → loss of retention and stability. Movement of dentures in function may result in: Resorption. Predisposition to candidal infection. Denture irritation hyperplasia. Inflammatory papillary hyperplasia of the palate. All of these are exacerbated by wear of the occlusal surfaces.

Miconazole gel can be added to the fitting surface of the denture before insertion. Coexisting papillary hyperplasia of palate may need surgical reduction. Systemic fluconazole may be used in some cases.

The possibility of an underlying condition predisposing to candidosis should be considered, especially if the infection involves other parts of the mouth or lips or if treatment fails despite good denture hygiene. In this case, referral to the patient's general practitioner would be indicated for further investigations.
Also known as denture sore mouth, a misnomer because the condition is usually symptomless. Classically, seen as redness of the palate under a F/− denture, with petechial and whitish areas.

problems.description: A sudden blood blister bursts onto the soft palate during a meal — alarming to the patient, with no prior warning.
problems.etiology: An acute, localised oral blood blister of unknown aetiology. The working theory is that trauma causes a break at the epithelium-connective tissue junction, leading to bleeding from superficial capillaries and formation of a bulla [1]. Steroid inhalers may predispose [1]. The event is characteristically sudden — there is no prodrome.
problems.presentation:
What happens is that the patient notices a sudden blood-filled blister appearing during eating, on the soft palate, cheek, or tongue [1]. It can be alarming — the blister may be sizeable and looks dramatic. Most common in elderly patients [1]. The blister ruptures quickly, leaving a shallow ulcer that heals uneventfully.

The soft palate, cheeks, and tongue are the most common sites [1].
problems.results:
Diagnosis is largely clinical — a sudden blood blister during eating in an elderly patient, resolving rapidly without scar, in the absence of any coagulation disorder. The key investigation step is excluding bullous conditions: pemphigus and pemphigoid can both produce oral blisters and are far more significant clinically [1].

If blisters are recurrent, persistent, or present at multiple sites, biopsy and haematological screen are warranted to exclude pemphigoid, pemphigus, and coagulation disorders.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The question to ask is whether this is truly a benign, isolated blood blister or whether it is an early presentation of pemphigus or mucous membrane pemphigoid. Angina bullosa haemorrhagica is distinguished by: sudden onset during eating, soft palate predominance, and the need to exclude other bullous conditions [1].
problems.treatment: Puncture the blister if it is causing discomfort, and reassure the patient [1]. The goal is to exclude pemphigus and pemphigoid — if any doubt exists, refer for biopsy and immunofluorescence. No specific treatment is needed for the blood blister itself.
problems.prognosis: Oral blood blisters are irritating but of no known significance in isolation [2]. Healing is rapid and scarring does not occur. The risk is misdiagnosis — failing to identify pemphigoid or pemphigus on the first encounter.

citations.quote: An acute, localized oral blood blister of unknown aetiology, although trauma may cause break in epithelium–connective tissue junction leading to bleeding from superficial capillaries and formation of a bulla. Invariably develops during eating and can be alarming to the patient. Most common in elderly. Steroid inhalers may predispose. Soft palate, cheeks, and tongue most common sites. ∆: exclude other bullous conditions. Rx: puncture &/or reassure (must differentiate from pemphigus/pemphigoid).
Oral blood blisters; irritating but of no known significance (…… Angina bullosa haemorrhagica, p. 444).

problems.description: Febrile child with small painful ulcers clustered on the uvula, soft palate, and fauces — no gingivitis, no hand or foot lesions.
problems.etiology: Caused by Coxsackie A virus, confined to children [1]. The virus produces a febrile illness with sore throat as the cardinal symptoms. Spread is by the faeco-oral route [1]. The interesting bit is its site specificity: the ulcers cluster on the uvula, palate, and fauces rather than the anterior mouth — that distribution is pathognomonic [1].
problems.presentation:
What you'll see in a child is fever, general upset, and sore throat with widespread small ulcers on the oral mucosa [1]. The site pattern is the key: ulcers are on the uvula, palate, and fauces — no gingivitis, which helps distinguish it from primary herpetic stomatitis [1]. The illness may be preceded by sore throat and conjunctivitis, and can be mistaken for teething in young children [1].

The source also notes a separate, related illness: hand, foot, and mouth disease, where Coxsackie A16 produces ulcers throughout the oral cavity together with a papular vesicular rash on hands and feet [2]. Herpangina does not have the hand and foot lesions.
problems.results:
Diagnosis is clinical — the site-specific ulcer pattern in a febrile child. No gingivitis on examination separates this from herpetic stomatitis. A brief illness of 3–5 days in one source [3] and 10–14 days in another [1] indicates a self-limiting course.

No special investigations are routinely needed.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The rule of thumb for site: herpangina is confined to the posterior mouth — uvula, soft palate, and fauces, with no gingivitis [1]. Hand, foot, and mouth disease shares the same viral family but distributes ulcers throughout the oral cavity and adds the exanthem on hands and feet [2].
problems.treatment: Soft diet and symptomatic relief [3]. The illness is self-limiting and no antiviral is needed.
problems.prognosis: Self-limiting. The febrile illness resolves within days and the ulcers heal without scarring [1][3].

citations.quote: Herpangina is caused by Coxsackie A virus, is confined to children, and presents with widespread small ulcers on the oral mucosa with fever and general upset. Clinically it resembles herpetic stomatitis, but is site pathognomonic, affecting uvula, palate, and fauces with no gingivitis. May be preceded by sore throat and conjunctivitis. Can also be mistaken as 'teething'. Self-limiting in 10–14 days. Spread by faeco-oral route.

This is caused by Coxsackie virus (usually A16, but less commonly types 5 and 10) and is similar to herpangina but the lesions are present throughout the oral cavity. A papular, vesicular rash appears on the hands and feet in conjunction with nasal congestion and oral mucosal vesicles. These break down, leaving painful superficial ulcers, particularly on the palate. The gingivae are rarely involved. It is self-limiting in 10–14 days.
Febrile illness with sore throat due to ulcers on soft palate and throat. Usually lasts about 3–5 days. Rx: soft diet.

problems.description: Deep, non-healing ulcer on the palate in a patient with a known or possible history of syphilis — the ulcer has necrotic edges and may be enlarging.
problems.etiology: Tertiary syphilis develops several years after the primary infection, in approximately 30% of patients who do not receive treatment [1]. The third-stage lesion is the gumma: a necrotic granulomatous reaction that forms and enlarges over time [1]. The palate and tongue are the favoured oral sites [1]. Tertiary syphilis is a multisystem disorder involving the central nervous system and causing vasculitis [1].
problems.presentation:
A necrotic ulcer on the palate, with a granulomatous, destructive character that enlarges progressively [1]. The patient may not have an obvious history of syphilis — the primary and secondary episodes may have been mild or unrecognised. The ulcer can perforate the palate if left untreated [1].

The lesions are non-infectious at this stage [1].
problems.results: Syphilis serology (VDRL, TPHA) is the key investigation. Biopsy would show necrotic granulomatous tissue. Third-stage lesions are non-infectious, so T. pallidum cannot be isolated from the site [1]. Refer to GUM medicine or infectious diseases for systemic investigation and treatment — tertiary syphilis causes CNS and vascular disease beyond the oral findings [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: What distinguishes this from other palatal ulcers is the history (known or suspected syphilis, absence of an obvious dental cause), the deeply necrotic granulomatous character, and the progressive enlargement with potential palatal perforation [1].
problems.treatment: Refer urgently to GUM medicine or infectious diseases. Systemic treatment of syphilis is required. Tertiary syphilis is a multisystem disorder with CNS and vascular consequences beyond the oral lesion [1].
problems.prognosis: Without treatment, the gumma continues to enlarge and can perforate the palate. Tertiary syphilis is a multisystem disorder with CNS and vascular consequences beyond the oral lesion [1]. With appropriate systemic treatment, the active granulomatous process is arrested.

citations.quote: 3° lesion. Develops several years later in 30% of patients and is marked by gumma formation. This is a necrotic granulomatous reaction usually affecting the palate or tongue, which enlarges and ulcerates and may lead to perforation of the palate. Lesions are non-infectious. Tertiary syphilis is a multisystem disorder causing CNS involvement and vasculitis.

problems.description: Dark, rapidly enlarging, irregular pigmented lesion on the palate — not linked to any previous trauma or benign cause.
problems.etiology: A rare but potentially lethal intraoral malignancy [1]. A rare non-pigmented variant also exists [1].
problems.presentation:
A dark, irregular lesion on the palate or oral mucosa that enlarges rapidly [1]. The colour is very dark and the outline is irregular — both features that should raise immediate concern.

The non-pigmented variant is the dangerous diagnostic pitfall: it lacks the dark colouration and can be mistaken for other mucosal lesions [1].
problems.results: Any dark, rapidly growing, irregular oral lesion requires urgent biopsy.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The rapid enlargement and very dark, irregular outline are the clinical hallmarks [1]. Kaposi's sarcoma is a vascular lesion (HHV-8-related) appearing in AIDS patients and is also dark/purplish, but is a different entity [2]. Any dark oral lesion that is growing should be treated as malignant until proven otherwise.
problems.treatment: Urgent referral is indicated — prognosis is poor [1].

citations.quote: Potentially lethal, relatively rare IO malignancy. Very dark, irregular outline, enlarges rapidly; poor prognosis. Rare variant is non-pigmented.
(…… Kaposi's sarcoma (KS), p. 478.) A HHV-8-related radiosensitive vascular tumour associated with AIDS.

problems.description: Papillated pink or white asymptomatic lumps on the palate or oral mucosa — patient may have a history of an STD or skin warts.
problems.etiology: HPV is the main aetiological factor [1]. True warts in the mouth are rare and are usually transmitted from skin warts. The condition is found in those with an STD or AIDS, but most patients have no such link [1]. Squamous papillomata are more common than true warts and appear in a similar clinical pattern.
problems.presentation: Multiple papillated pink or white lumps that are asymptomatic [1]. The papillated surface texture — like a small cauliflower — is the identifying feature. The patient often notices them incidentally or they are found on routine examination. Lesions may be single or multiple.
problems.results:
- **Clinical appearance** of multiple papillated pink or white lumps is often enough for a working diagnosis [1].
- **Excision biopsy** is both the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic step. If on a stalk, ligate or diathermy the base — these lesions contain a prominent vessel [1].
- **HIV testing** if multiple lesions are present and no other risk factor is identified.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The papillated texture separates warts and papillomata from flat white patches (leukoplakia, candidosis) and from palatal nodules with smooth surfaces (torus, salivary gland tumours). The key clinical rule is that even though these lesions are HPV-driven and usually benign, excision biopsy is the correct management — it provides histological confirmation and removes the lesion in one step [1].
problems.treatment: Excision biopsy. If on a stalk, ligate or use diathermy at the base because these lesions contain a prominent vessel [1]. Screen for STD and HIV if the clinical context suggests it.
problems.prognosis: Excision is curative for individual lesions. In immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS), recurrence is more likely. The prognosis is generally good for isolated papillomata in immunocompetent patients.

citations.quote: The main aetiological factor is HPV. True warts are rare in the mouth and usually transmitted from skin warts. Found in those with a STD or AIDS, but most have no such link. Papillomata are common in the mouth; they appear as multiple papillated pink or white asymptomatic lumps. Rx: excision biopsy (if on a stalk—ligate or diathermy base as they contain a prominent vessel).

problems.description: Small pinpoint red spots on the soft palate — appearing in a child or young adult with a platelet disorder, febrile illness, or a history of forceful vomiting.
problems.conditionName: Palatal petechiae (thrombocytopenic purpura and associated causes)
problems.etiology: Purpura is due to platelet deficiency [1]. The commonest form in children is idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) [1]. Palatal petechiae can also appear in glandular fever, rubella, HIV, and recurrent vomiting — all contexts where there is either a coagulation disturbance or local capillary trauma [1].
problems.presentation: Pinpoint haemorrhages visible on the soft palate as red or dark-red spots — petechiae [1]. They do not blanch on pressure. The patient may have no oral complaint; the petechiae are often found incidentally, or the patient presents with the systemic illness. Spontaneous gingival bleeding may also be present in thrombocytopenic states.
problems.results: The interesting bit is that petechiae alone signal a need for urgent blood work. A full blood count with platelet count is the first step. If glandular fever is suspected, appropriate testing follows.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Palatal petechiae are almost never an isolated finding — they point to a systemic cause. The differential is broader than just ITP: glandular fever, rubella, HIV, and vomiting-related capillary trauma can all produce the same picture [1]. The clinical question is always: what is the underlying cause? Never reassure and discharge on the appearance of palatal petechiae alone without a haematological screen.
problems.treatment: The goal is to identify and treat the underlying cause. Refer to the GP or haematology urgently if platelet deficiency is suspected.
problems.prognosis: Depends entirely on the underlying condition [1]. ITP in children often resolves spontaneously. HIV and glandular fever carry their own prognosis. The palatal petechiae themselves resolve as the systemic condition is managed.

citations.quote: Purpura is due to platelet deficiency. Commonest as idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in children. Palatal petechiae or bruising may be seen. Palatal petechiae are also seen in glandular fever, rubella, HIV, and recurrent vomiting.

problems.description: Unusually high-arched narrow palate in a very tall, thin patient with long fingers — referred for dental care or found at routine examination.
problems.etiology: An autosomal dominant condition [1]. The syndrome is characterised by a connective tissue abnormality that produces skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular features. Joint laxity is a feature, and the high-arched palate arises from the altered connective tissue architecture [1].
problems.presentation:
What you'll see is a tall, thin patient with arachnodactyly — long, thin, spider-like hands [1]. The high-arched palate is often an incidental finding during a dental examination. Other features include dislocation of the lens, and cardiovascular anomalies: dissecting aneurysms of the thoracic aorta, aortic regurgitation, and floppy mitral valve [1]. Joint laxity is also common [1].

The condition is highly prevalent among top-class basketball and volleyball players [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical and genetic. On examination: high-arched palate, arachnodactyly. Cardiovascular assessment is essential — aortic dissection and valvular disease are the life-threatening risks [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of high-arched palate, arachnodactyly, and tall thin stature is distinctive [1]. The reason Marfan syndrome matters in dental practice is the cardiovascular risk. Joint laxity and lens dislocation are additional pointers if the history is taken properly [1].
problems.treatment: The oral finding requires no direct treatment. Refer for cardiovascular assessment and genetic counselling if Marfan syndrome is suspected and not yet diagnosed [1].
problems.prognosis: The risk of aortic dissection and cardiovascular complications determines long-term prognosis [1]. The dental finding of a high-arched palate is in itself benign.

citations.quote: An autosomal dominant condition characterized by tall, thin stature and arachnodactyly (long, thin, spider-like hands), dislocation of the lens, dissecting aneurysms of the thoracic aorta, aortic regurgitation, floppy mitral valve, and high-arched palate. Joint laxity is also common. This condition is highly prevalent among top-class basketball and volleyball players, for obvious reasons.

problems.description: Cleft palate in a child with a flat mid-face, severe myopia, and early-onset arthropathy — the cleft was the presenting feature at birth.
problems.etiology: Stickler syndrome is perhaps the commonest syndrome associated with cleft palate [1]. The syndrome consists of flat mid-face, cleft palate (in 20% of cases), myopia, retinal detachment, hearing loss (in 80%), and arthropathy [1]. About 30% of Robin sequence patients have Stickler syndrome [1]. The reason the eye examination matters is that retinal detachment is a serious risk and can be missed if not actively looked for [1].
problems.presentation: A child with a cleft palate who also has a flat mid-face and significant myopia. The cleft palate is typically the presenting oral feature. Hearing loss is present in 80% [1], and arthropathy may emerge later in childhood. In some patients the syndrome is first recognised when the cleft palate is investigated and the examiner notes the characteristic flat facies and eye findings.
problems.results: The key investigation is ophthalmological examination to look for retinal detachment [1]. Hearing assessment is needed in all cases, given the 80% rate of hearing loss [1]. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. For the cleft palate itself, the same specialist team referral applies as for any cleft (cleft surgeon, speech therapist, ENT, orthodontist).
problems.definingCharacteristics: The takeaway for practice is this: about 30% of Robin sequence cases have Stickler syndrome, so any child with Robin sequence should have their eyes examined [1]. Among syndromic cleft palate diagnoses, Stickler stands out for the severity and frequency of its ocular involvement — retinal detachment is vision-threatening and requires proactive surveillance [1].
problems.treatment: Refer to a specialist cleft team for palate repair. Ophthalmology referral is mandatory to assess retinal status [1]. Audiology assessment for hearing loss [1]. Ongoing orthopaedic or rheumatology input for arthropathy as the child grows.
problems.prognosis: Cleft palate itself has good surgical outcomes when managed by a specialist team. The prognostic concerns are ocular — retinal detachment can cause blindness if not detected and treated — and auditory, given the 80% hearing loss rate [1].

citations.quote: Perhaps the commonest syndrome associated with cleft palate (20%). Consists of flat mid-face, cleft palate, myopia, retinal detachment, hearing loss (80%), and arthropathy. About 30% of Robin sequence patients have Stickler syndrome, therefore examine eyes.

problems.description: Cleft palate in a child with a flattened face, multiple congenital joint dislocations, and short stature — the dislocations are present at birth.
problems.etiology: A mainly autosomal dominant condition with a predilection for females [1]. The syndrome combines cleft palate with flattened facies, multiple congenital joint dislocations, foot deformities, and short stature [1]. The larynx may also be affected [1]. Cleft palate in this context is one of a constellation of connective tissue and skeletal abnormalities present from birth.
problems.presentation: At birth: the combination of multiple congenital joint dislocations together with cleft palate and a flattened face is the presenting picture [1]. The dislocations are typically of major joints (hips, knees, elbows) and are present from birth, which is the feature that distinguishes Larsen from other cleft syndromes. Sufferers are usually of short stature [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical and radiological — multiple joint dislocations confirmed on skeletal survey. Genetic testing may confirm the diagnosis. For dental management, the cleft palate follows standard cleft team assessment and repair.
problems.definingCharacteristics: What makes Larsen syndrome distinctive among cleft palate syndromes is the multiple congenital joint dislocations present at birth [1]. Stickler syndrome also includes cleft palate and connective tissue involvement, but its hallmark is severe myopia and retinal detachment rather than major joint dislocations. Marfan syndrome has joint laxity but not fixed congenital dislocations, and its palate finding is a high arch rather than a cleft. Larsen's picture — cleft + flattened facies + birth dislocations — is the defining cluster [1].
problems.treatment: Specialist cleft team referral for the cleft palate [1]. Orthopaedic management for the multiple joint dislocations — these are the dominant functional challenge in infancy and childhood. Laryngeal involvement may require ENT assessment [1].
problems.prognosis: Depends on the severity of orthopaedic involvement and the presence of laryngeal anomalies [1]. Cleft palate itself has a good surgical prognosis with specialist team management. Long-term orthopaedic and developmental input is typically needed.

citations.quote: A mainly autosomal dominant condition, with a predilection for females, consisting of cleft palate, flattened facies, multiple congenital dislocations, and deformities of the feet. Sufferers are usually of short stature. Larynx may be affected.
